title: Questioning Your Own Sources
answer: Questioning your own sources means treating every paper, claim, and model output as provisional until its provenance, method, and conflicts have been checked. In literature review and evidence synthesis, this includes verifying that a source actually supports the claim attributed to it, that the study design fits the question, and that the paper has not been retracted or corrected. crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Questioning your own sources means treating every paper, claim, and model output as provisional until its provenance, method, and conflicts have been checked. In literature review and evidence synthesis, this includes verifying that a source actually supports the claim attributed to it, that the study design fits the question, and that the paper has not been retracted or corrected. On this site, that work starts from the original paper rather than a secondary summary, and the 10,916 extracted claims are treated as leads to verify, not as settled fact.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on a curated evidence base of 135 research papers, 91 AI books, 803 scientific models, 732 AI tools, and 674 glossary terms, with claims extracted directly from the papers. The site does not link to the Consensus search tool; it links to the original paper so the reader can inspect the methods, data, and limitations directly. A reference manager or a plain spreadsheet is often enough, but the key infrastructure is the link between each claim and the exact passage or figure in the source.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: For each source, you check the authors, venue, date, funding, and sample or dataset, then compare the claim you want to use against the paper's actual results section. You look for overstatement, small samples, conflicts of interest, and citation chains that misquote earlier work. When a claim appears in the extracted set, you trace it back to the original paper and read the surrounding context rather than accepting the summary.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: The main risks are propagating a retracted or corrected finding, citing a preprint as if it were peer reviewed, or repeating a claim that the original authors did not make. Provenance means keeping the DOI, version, and access date for every source, and noting whether the source is a preprint, conference paper, journal article, or book chapter. Rights issues are usually about fair quotation and not reproducing large excerpts, but the larger governance duty is to flag uncertainty and correct your own reference list when a source changes.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Source checking is moving toward semi-automated claim verification, where a model can flag mismatches between a claim and the cited passage, detect retractions, and suggest alternative studies. The site's extracted claims and model catalogue point toward tools that compare a draft's citations against the underlying papers, but the final judgment still belongs to the researcher. Expect more emphasis on versioned evidence, living reviews, and audit trails that show exactly which version of a paper supported which conclusion.
